newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan seen tightening liquidity on red-hot stocks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan seen tightening liquidity on red-hot stocks.

text.p: Taiwan's solid March money supply growth reflected the island's sizzling stock market and intensified the need for the central bank to tighten funds to prevent over-exuberance by the bourse, economists said Friday.

Taiwan's broadest money supply measure, M2, grew 9.90 percent in March from a year earlier, the third successive month that the figure fell into the central bank's target zone of 9-14 percent, the central bank said late on Thursday.
The bank also announced that March's M1B supply grew 14.44 percent year-on-year, up sharply from the 4-6 percent growths seen regularly just a few months ago.
Economists said the high M1B growth indicated that investors were actively transferring their money from banks' time deposits to passbook savings accounts in order to make stock investments.
"Such high M1B growth likely will force the central bank to continue moves to tighten liquidity in a bid to cool the red-hot stock market," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
The Taiwan stock index has risen more than 80 percent since February 1996, when the market was beset by tensions between Taiwan and rival China.
The index has surged 25 percent in 1997 alone, and it capped a five-session bull run on Friday by closing 24.96 points, or 0.29 percent, higher at 8,654.19.
The central bank has repeatedly issued negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) in recent months to mop up excess liquidity -- a move that analysts said was intended to cool the stock market.

"The central bank has been trying hard to cool off the stock market, having taken back some T$100 billion (US$3.6 billion) through NCD issues away from the market in the past three and a half months," Norman Yin, banking professor at National Chengchi University, told Reuters Financial Television.
The central bank's NCD issues helped push up Taiwan's overnight interbank rate to above 6.0 percent recently, much higher than a targeted short-term rate zone of 5.0-5.5 percent.
The rate stood at 6.366 percent at mid-session on Friday.
But economists said the central bank's NCD issues have not affected the bourse, and they recommended other measures.
"The NCD issues have so far had little effect. The government instead should accelerate adding chip (share) supplies for the stock market in order to effectively cool the market," Yin said.
The government can increase the number of shares in the market by approving more listings of private companies and by accelerating privatisation of state-run firms, Yin said.
But economists said they did not expect the central bank to launch additional measures to tighten liquidity at the forthcoming central bank board meeting on May 8.
"To boost the still slowly recovering economy, the central bank has little room to hike rediscount rate or other rates," said Terry Chen, vice-president of Grand Cathay Securities.
"It is expected to maintain its stable-to-loose, but not too loose, monetary policy in its board meeting," Chen said.
However, economists said they also did not expect the central bank to loosen policy to boost the economy due to concerns that the stock market would over-rally.
The central bank has said it has no plans to discuss lowering banks' reserve requirements at its board meeting.
"It is not an appropriate time to lower reserve requirements. The central bank has no plans to discuss it during the May 8 board meeting," deputy central bank governor Hsu Chia-tung said on Monday.
